stages.title: Urban planning
stages.hook: Kestrel Bay can add 30,000 homes by spreading outward or by building up near its stations. Which is better, and by what measure?
explain: Urban planning shapes how land is used so that a city can function: where people live, work, shop, learn and move. Its main tools are plans, zoning codes, density limits, design standards and the timing of infrastructure. Powers are shared differently between national, regional and local governments around the world.

Density is people (or homes) per unit of land. Floor area ratio (FAR) is total building floor area divided by plot area. Higher density can shorten trips, lower the cost per home of pipes and roads, and make public transport viable. It can also raise concerns about congestion, light and local character. Low density protects space but increases travel and infrastructure cost per household.

Mixed-use zoning combines homes, shops and workplaces so more daily needs are within walking distance. Transit-oriented development concentrates growth near stations. Planners judge such ideas against stated criteria: access to services, cost to the city, housing supply, environmental impact and public acceptance. Evidence and context matter; there is no single ideal form.

example.q: A 2,000 m² plot has a permitted FAR of 3.0. What is the maximum total floor area, and how many 75 m² flats fit if 20% of floor area is used for corridors and services?

analogies.home: Packing a suitcase tightly lets you carry more but makes it harder to find things. Density has similar trade-offs.
analogies.farm: Planting rows closer gives a bigger harvest per hectare but needs more water and care per plant.
analogies.sea: A port that packs more berths into a harbour moves more cargo but needs better traffic control.
analogies.tech: Compact data centres are efficient but need strong cooling and planning.

stages.mnemonic: Where, how much, what mix, how connected: Location, Density, Mix, Links.
terms: Total floor area divided by plot area.
Zoning that allows homes, shops and workplaces together.
Growth concentrated near public transport stops.
Low-density growth spreading outward from a city.

misc.wrong: There is one perfect city form that every place should copy.
misc.right: Good form depends on geography, culture, climate, budget and goals; planners compare options with criteria.

stages.limits: Research on density's effects is context-dependent, and planners disagree about how dense is best.

trip.prompt: Find how floor area ratio is used in zoning and give one example calculation.

questions.q: What does floor area ratio measure?
o: Total floor area divided by plot area
The number of residents served by each bus
Total property tax collected per square metre
The height of a building compared with its neighbours
questions.why: FAR compares total building floor space with plot size.

questions.q: Which is a typical benefit of mixed-use zoning?
o: More daily needs within walking distance
Longer commutes for most workers
Fewer shops and services nearby
Homes kept far away from jobs and shops
questions.why: Mixing uses shortens everyday trips.

questions.q: A district adds homes far from transit and services. What is a likely cost to the city?
o: Higher cost per household for roads, pipes and services
Shorter average travel distance for all
Cheaper bus service for every route
No extra cost, since services come free
questions.why: Spread-out areas need more infrastructure per household.

questions.q: Residents worry that a tall building will block light. Which response best reflects good planning?
o: Model shadow effects and weigh them against housing and transport benefits
Ignore the concern because light is not a planning matter
Ban every tall building in the city automatically
Approve it at once without studying any effects
questions.why: Evidence-based impact assessment lets planners weigh the trade-off.

questions.q: Which statement about density is most accurate?
o: Its effects depend on design, services and context
Higher density is always better for every city
Lower density is always better for every city
Density has no effects on services or travel
questions.why: Evidence shows effects vary with context.

questions.q: A 5,000 m² plot has an allowed FAR of 2.4. What is the maximum total floor area in m²?
Kestrel Bay has 45,000 residents on 18 km² of urban land. What is the density in people per km²?
Match each tool to its purpose.
pairs: Caps homes or floor area per plot
Shapes how buildings look and function
Times pipes and roads with growth
questions.why: Planners use rules, limits, standards and timing together.

questions.q: Give one argument for and one against concentrating new homes near train stations.
questions.model: For: more people can use public transport and walk, which cuts car trips and makes services viable. Against: higher density may bring crowding, shading, higher land prices or changes to local character, so impacts need managing.
questions.why: A balanced answer names a benefit and a cost.

questions.q: Which indicator best measures whether a plan improves access?
o: Share of residents within a 15-minute walk of key services
The number of plan drawings produced each year
The height of the tallest building in the plan
The number of public meetings that were held
questions.why: Access is measured by how easily people can reach services.

panel.q: Two reasonable plans exist: Plan P spreads growth with large lots, Plan Q concentrates growth near stations. Which approach is most defensible?
o: Score both against stated criteria with evidence and consult residents
Choose the plan that the loudest group of residents supports most
Choose the plan with the lower first-year cost only, ignoring later costs
Choose the plan that the mayor sketched first, as it is the leader's
panel.why: Stated criteria and evidence give a non-partisan basis.

panel.q: Why can a plan that raises housing supply still fail to deliver affordability for lower-income households?
panel.model: If new homes are priced at the high end of the market and no affordable units or subsidies are included, lower-income households may still be unable to pay, so the mix of home types and support tools matters.
panel.why: Supply helps but needs the right mix and tools.

panel.q: Why should plans include phasing of infrastructure?
o: Services should arrive when homes are occupied
Roads should be built and then left to wait ten years
Homes can safely stay empty for many years first
Phasing of infrastructure is not allowed by law
panel.why: Timing avoids gaps where residents lack services.

teach.model: Urban planning decides how land is used for homes, jobs, shops and roads. Tools include zoning and density limits. Planners compare designs such as dense or spread-out growth using criteria like access, cost and environment, because no single form suits every city.

points.ask: How do planners choose between designs?
Is there one best city form?

stages.title: Public procurement
stages.hook: A city needs 12 electric buses. Bidder A is cheapest. Bidder B costs 8% more but promises lower running costs. How should the city decide, and how can it prevent favouritism?
explain: Public procurement is how governments buy goods, services and works using public money. Because the amounts are large, rules aim to deliver value for money, fair competition and honesty. Typical principles are transparency, equal treatment of bidders, non-discrimination and accountability.

Procedures often require open tendering above a set threshold, published criteria and weights set before bids arrive, and a record of the evaluation. Choosing only the lowest price can backfire if quality is poor or running costs are high. Many systems therefore use best-value or lowest life-cycle cost, which includes purchase price, operating costs and disposal.

Procurement is a corruption risk. Red flags include tailor-made specifications, repeated winners who bid in rotation, unusually similar bids (possible bid rigging), unexplained contract changes and undeclared conflicts of interest. Safeguards include open data on contracts, independent evaluators, declaring interests, audits and complaint channels. Legal details differ between countries.

example.q: Criteria: price 60%, quality 40%. Bid A scores price 80, quality 70. Bid B scores price 70, quality 90. Which wins?

analogies.home: Buying a cheap printer that eats expensive ink can cost more than a pricier one with cheap ink.
analogies.farm: A farmer comparing tractors looks at fuel use and repairs, not only the sticker price.
analogies.sport: A club picking a stadium builder checks quality and track record, not just the lowest quote.
analogies.city: Publishing the scoring rules before bids is like a referee announcing the rules before kick-off.

terms: A formal invitation to bid for a contract.
Total cost over an asset's life: buying, running, disposing.
When personal interests could affect an official duty.

misc.wrong: The cheapest bid is always the best value.
misc.right: Value for money considers quality, risk and life-cycle cost as well as price.

stages.limits: Thresholds, rules and balance between price and quality vary by country, and too many rules can slow purchasing.

trip.prompt: Find the main stages of a public tender and the purpose of each.

questions.q: What is the purpose of publishing evaluation criteria before bids arrive?
o: It makes the process fair and transparent
It helps bidders copy each other's offers
It hides how the winners are chosen from the public
It makes the tenders much shorter and faster
questions.why: Known criteria prevent changing the rules to favour someone.

questions.q: Which is a red flag for bid rigging?
o: Several bids are almost identical and winners seem to take turns
Bids vary widely in price from firm to firm
A bidder asks a clarifying question before the deadline
Bids are opened in public on the stated date
questions.why: Similar bids and rotation suggest coordination.

questions.q: A councillor owns shares in a bidding firm. What should happen?
o: Declare the interest and step out of the decision
Say nothing and stay in the meeting
Vote for the firm to help it win
Hide the shares so no one finds out about them
questions.why: Conflicts of interest must be declared and managed.

questions.q: Bus X costs 400,000 luns and costs 60,000 a year to run for 10 years. Bus Y costs 480,000 and costs 40,000 a year for 10 years. On life-cycle cost, which is better?
o: Bus Y
Bus X
They are equal
Cannot be compared

questions.q: Why does procurement matter for the whole economy?
o: Governments buy large amounts, so rules affect competition and costs
It sets the exchange rates between currencies
It decides the results of national elections
It chooses the school curriculum for all children
questions.why: Public purchasing is a large share of spending in many economies.

questions.q: Criteria: price 70%, quality 30%. A bid scores 60 on price and 90 on quality. What is its weighted score?
A contract is 5,000,000 luns. A change order adds 1,250,000 luns. By what percentage did the cost grow?
Put the stages of a competitive tender in order.
items: Evaluate bids using the published criteria
questions.why: Criteria come before bids; monitoring follows award.

questions.q: Explain why the lowest bid can end up costing the city more.
questions.model: A very low bid may have poor quality, hidden extras or high running costs, leading to repairs, delays or change orders that cost more than a better-priced bid, so life-cycle cost should be compared.
questions.why: Value for money is about total cost and quality.

questions.q: Which safeguard best deters corruption in procurement?
o: Open publication of contracts with independent audits
Keeping all contracts secret from the public
Allowing single-source awards as the default choice
Letting evaluators work alone and in private
questions.why: Transparency and independent checks reduce opportunities.

panel.q: In an emergency, a city needs generators within 48 hours and skips the open tender. Which safeguard is most appropriate?
o: Use a limited process, document reasons and review it afterward
Do it in secret so that rivals cannot object
Avoid keeping any record, to save time and effort
Pick a friend's firm because it can deliver fastest
panel.why: Emergency exceptions should be limited, documented and reviewed.

panel.q: A small local firm bids slightly higher than a distant large firm. Should the city give local firms a preference? Give one consideration on each side.
panel.model: A preference can keep spending and jobs local, but it can reduce competition and raise costs, and some rules limit discrimination, so the city should weigh value for money and legal rules and publish the criteria.
panel.why: A balanced answer weighs benefits and costs; the question is contested.

panel.q: Why use independent evaluators?
o: To reduce bias and favouritism
To lengthen the process
To increase costs deliberately
To avoid records
panel.why: Independence supports fair assessment.

teach.model: Procurement is how governments buy things with public money. Fair rules include open tenders, published criteria and declared interests. The best bid is the one with the best value, including running costs, not always the cheapest. Transparency and audits help prevent corruption.

stages.title: Municipal budgeting
stages.hook: Kestrel Bay's departments request 140 million luns but revenue is 120 million. Who gets cut, and how can the process stay fair and open?
explain: A municipal budget turns plans into numbers. It usually has an operating budget (running services, paid mostly from recurring revenue) and a capital budget (long-lived assets, often financed partly by borrowing). Many cities pass a balanced operating budget by law; rules on borrowing differ by country.

Budget formats vary. Line-item budgets list inputs like wages. Performance-based budgets link money to results, such as response times. Participatory budgeting lets residents help decide how part of the money is spent. Whichever format is used, a good process publishes proposals, shows assumptions and explains changes.

Resilience measures matter. Reserves (savings) cover shocks, and are often described in months of spending. The debt service ratio, which is debt payments as a share of revenue, shows how much revenue is already committed. Leaders compare options on criteria such as fiscal sustainability, access to services and evidence of effectiveness, not on preferences alone.

example.q: Reserves are 18 million luns and monthly operating spending is 6 million. How many months of spending are covered? If debt payments are 9 million of 120 million revenue, what is the debt service ratio?
steps: 7.5% of revenue is committed to debt payments.
example.a: 3 months of reserves; debt service ratio 7.5%.

analogies.home: A household keeps an emergency fund and avoids spending more than it can repay each month.
analogies.farm: A farmer saves part of a good harvest to survive a drought.
analogies.sport: A club spends wages from regular income and saves for injuries.
analogies.tech: Teams reserve capacity so a traffic spike does not crash the system.

terms: Money for running services each year.
Money for building or buying long-lasting assets.
Debt payments as a share of revenue.

misc.wrong: A budget surplus always means the city is well run.
misc.right: A surplus could reflect underspending on needed services or deferred maintenance; results must be checked.

stages.limits: Budget rules, borrowing limits and reserve targets differ across countries, and experts disagree on the best reserve level.

trip.prompt: Find an example city and what share of its budget residents decided.

questions.q: Which is part of a capital budget?
o: Building a new water treatment plant
Paying monthly salaries to city staff
Buying printer paper for the council offices
Paying the electricity bills for city buildings
questions.why: Capital budgets fund long-lived assets.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of reserves?
o: To cover shocks and shortfalls
To avoid having to plan ahead at all
To pay for waste in the everyday budget
To hide spending from the public auditors
questions.why: Reserves protect services during emergencies or revenue drops.

questions.q: What does a performance-based budget add?
o: A link between funding and measured results
A ban on all kinds of spending by the city
Only a list of the salaries paid to staff
A secret account that no one can inspect
questions.why: It ties resources to outputs and outcomes.

questions.q: A city has a surplus because it delayed all road repairs. What is the concern?
o: Costs are being pushed to the future and may grow
Surpluses are always bad and must be avoided
Roads repair themselves if they are left alone long enough
The surplus is illegal under all budget rules
questions.why: Deferred maintenance can raise later costs.

questions.q: Which makes a budget process more transparent?
o: Publishing proposals, assumptions and reasons for changes
Passing the budget late at night with few present
Keeping all drafts secret until the vote is over
Using unexplained codes for the spending lines
questions.why: Open information lets people understand and challenge choices.

questions.q: Reserves are 24 million luns and monthly operating spending is 8 million luns. How many months of spending do reserves cover?
Revenue is 150 million luns and debt payments are 12 million luns. What is the debt service ratio as a percentage?
Departments request 140 million luns but revenue is 120 million. By what percentage do requests exceed revenue (to one decimal place)?
Put these budget-cycle steps in order.
questions.why: The cycle moves from estimates to decision to accountability.

questions.q: Requests exceed revenue by 20 million luns. Describe a fair, non-partisan way to decide what to cut or delay.
questions.model: State criteria in advance such as safety, legal duties, access, effectiveness and cost, score each request using evidence, consult residents, and publish the reasons for what was funded or delayed.
questions.why: Transparent criteria and evidence make the choice defensible.

panel.q: A council funds a popular festival by using reserves for recurring salaries. What is the fiscal-sustainability concern?
o: Reserves are one-time while salaries recur
Festivals are illegal in a public budget under law
Salaries should never be paid by a city council
Reserves can never be used for any purpose
panel.why: Using one-time money for recurring costs creates a future gap.

panel.q: Participatory budgeting lets residents decide part of the budget. Give one strength and one limitation.
panel.model: It builds trust and uses local knowledge, but it usually covers only a small share of the budget and the people who take part may not represent everyone, so extra outreach is needed.
panel.why: Balanced assessment of a contested tool.

panel.q: Why compare budgets per resident across years?
o: It adjusts for population changes
It hides the effects of inflation on prices
It shows what the weather was like each year
It removes all the debt from the accounts
panel.why: Per-capita figures make comparisons fairer.

teach.model: A municipal budget turns plans into money decisions, with an operating part for running services and a capital part for lasting assets. Good budgets are published, keep reserves, and choose priorities using clear criteria and evidence.

points.ask: What are the two main parts?

stages.title: Public infrastructure management
stages.hook: Resurfacing a road now costs 100,000 luns per km. Wait ten years and it needs a full rebuild at 600,000. Why do cities still put repairs off?
explain: Infrastructure management, often called asset management, treats roads, pipes, bridges and buildings as assets with a life cycle: plan, build or buy, operate, maintain, renew and dispose. The aim is to deliver the required service at the lowest sensible life-cycle cost and acceptable risk.

Maintenance is cheaper if done on time. Small repairs prevent faster decay, a pattern often described by condition curves. Deferred maintenance creates a backlog, which is a hidden liability: the work is owed but not yet paid. Cities keep asset registers and condition scores, and rank work by risk (likelihood and consequence of failure) and by benefit per luns spent.

Management also covers funding rules, such as setting aside money for renewal, and data such as leak reports and bridge inspections. Fairness matters: neglected neighbourhoods may suffer more failures. Climate and technology change requirements, so plans are reviewed regularly.

example.q: A city has 25 km of road. Resurfacing on time costs 100,000 luns per km. Waiting causes reconstruction at 600,000 luns per km. What does acting on time save across the 25 km?

analogies.home: Oiling a squeaky door hinge is cheap; replacing the whole door is not.
analogies.farm: Fixing a small fence gap protects the herd; waiting until animals escape costs far more.
analogies.sea: Repainting a ship's hull on schedule prevents rust that would need major repairs.
analogies.tech: Updating software regularly avoids a costly system rebuild after failure.

stages.mnemonic: Know, Rank, Fix early, Renew: the asset cycle.
terms: Managing assets over their whole life to give required service at lowest sensible cost.
Repairs postponed, building up future cost.
A rating of how good or poor an asset is.
Likelihood of failure times its consequence.

misc.right: It usually moves cost to the future, often at a higher price, and can raise safety risks.

stages.limits: Decay rates and costs differ by climate, materials and use, so the numbers here are illustrative.

trip.prompt: Find how organisations rank infrastructure work by risk and consequence.

questions.q: What is deferred maintenance?
o: Repairs postponed that build up future cost
Repairs that are done early to save money later
A new building put up in place of an old one
A type of tax charged on old buildings
questions.why: It is work owed but not yet done.

questions.q: Why rank projects by both likelihood and consequence of failure?
o: A rare failure of a critical asset can matter more than a common minor one
Likelihood alone is enough to rank every project
Consequence of failure is irrelevant when ranking projects
It makes the project lists longer and more complete
questions.why: Risk combines probability and impact.

questions.q: A pipe network has frequent bursts in an older district. What should managers do first?
o: Use condition and failure data to target replacement
Ignore the area until the bursts stop on their own
Replace the whole network citywide at once
Raise the water fee in that district only, as a penalty
questions.why: Data-guided targeting uses limited money best.

questions.q: What is life-cycle cost?
o: Total cost of owning an asset over its life
Only the cost of constructing the asset at first
Only the cost of repairing the asset when it breaks
The cost of the land the asset sits on
questions.why: It includes build, operate, maintain and dispose.

questions.q: Why might neglected neighbourhoods need explicit attention in asset plans?
o: They may suffer more failures and have fewer voices
They always have the newest pipes and roads in the city
They never use the services the city provides
They pay no tax to the city at all
questions.why: Equity requires checking who bears risks.

questions.q: Resurfacing costs 100,000 luns per km on time or 600,000 per km if delayed. For 40 km, how many luns are saved by acting on time?
A bridge costs 24,000,000 luns and is expected to last 60 years. What is the straight-line cost per year in luns?
Put the asset life-cycle stages in order.
questions.why: Assets are planned, built, used and maintained, renewed, then disposed.

questions.q: A city must choose between fixing three bridges. Which criteria could rank them fairly?
questions.model: Use the bridges' condition and risk of failure, how many people depend on them, the consequences of closure and the cost of repair, then rank by benefit per luns and explain the ranking.
questions.why: Clear criteria and data justify prioritisation.

questions.q: If the maintenance backlog is growing each year, what does it indicate?
o: Renewal spending is below what is needed
The assets are steadily getting better each year
Taxes are always too low in the city
It indicates nothing useful about the assets at all
questions.why: Backlog growth means underinvestment relative to need.

panel.q: A city has 10 million luns for repairs. Option 1 resurfaces many busy roads cheaply. Option 2 rebuilds one failing bridge. How should leaders decide?
o: Compare risk reduction and benefit per luns using condition data
Choose the option closest to the mayor's own street
Always choose the bigger project because it helps more
Always choose the cheaper project whatever the risk
panel.why: Risk-based comparison supports a defensible decision.

panel.q: Why might a city be tempted to defer maintenance, and what does that do to future budgets?
panel.model: Deferring saves money now and new projects are more visible, but the work becomes larger and costlier later, creating a backlog that future budgets must pay.
panel.why: Short-term incentives can create long-term costs.

panel.q: Which data improves asset decisions most?
o: Regular condition inspections and failure records
Rumours that are passed around among residents
Advertising from firms that sell repair materials
Guesses made by officials with no inspection
panel.why: Good data supports good decisions.

teach.model: Infrastructure management looks after roads, pipes and buildings over their whole life. Doing maintenance on time is usually cheaper than rebuilding later. Managers use condition data and risk to decide what to fix first.

stages.title: Transport systems
stages.hook: A bus rapid transit line costs a fraction of a metro per kilometre, but a metro carries more. Which should Kestrel Bay build?
explain: A transport system is a network of modes: walking, cycling, buses, trams, trains, cars and freight. Planners aim for access to jobs and services, safety, reliability, affordability and low environmental impact, within a budget. The 'modal share' is the percentage of trips made by each mode.

Modes differ in capacity and cost. Bus rapid transit (BRT) uses dedicated lanes and stations and costs much less per kilometre than metro or rail, while a metro can carry far more passengers per hour at high cost. Choices depend on demand, geography and funding. A comparison metric is cost per passenger trip over the asset's life.

Roads fill up when demand exceeds capacity. Adding lanes can attract more traffic, called induced demand, so congestion may return. Tools to manage demand include road pricing, parking policy, bus priority and better walking and cycling routes. Congestion pricing is debated: supporters cite less traffic and revenue; critics cite fairness and effects on lower-income drivers, so designs often include discounts or reinvest revenue in transport alternatives.

example.q: A BRT line is 12 km at 15 million luns/km. A metro on the same corridor is 12 km at 120 million luns/km. What is the difference in capital cost?

analogies.home: A family decides between a bike, a van and a bus pass based on trips, cost and number of people.
analogies.sea: A harbour uses ferries for short crossings and big ships for long hauls.
analogies.sport: A stadium needs entrances sized to the crowd, not to the average day.
analogies.nature: A river with a wider channel carries more water, but only to a point before flooding.

stages.mnemonic: Mode, Money, Demand, Reach: choose the mode that fits the demand.
terms: The percentage of trips made by each mode.
Extra traffic caused by new road capacity.
Bus service with dedicated lanes and stations.
A charge for using roads at busy times.

misc.wrong: Building more road lanes always ends congestion.
misc.right: Extra capacity can attract more traffic, so demand management and alternatives matter.

stages.limits: Effects of pricing and new roads vary by city, and transport economists disagree on how large induced demand is in each case.

trip.prompt: Find a city that built BRT and note its reported cost and passenger numbers.

questions.q: What is modal share?
o: The percentage of trips made by each mode
The width of a road measured in metres
The price of a single ticket on each route
The average age of the buses in the fleet
questions.why: It shows how people travel.

questions.q: What is induced demand?
o: Extra traffic that appears after road capacity increases
A tax charged on every litre of petrol
A cut in bus fares meant to attract riders
The timing pattern of traffic lights at junctions
questions.why: New capacity can attract more users.

questions.q: Which factor most favours a metro over BRT?
o: Very high passenger demand along a dense corridor
Low passenger demand along a quiet corridor
A very small budget for building new lines
Few riders spread across a wide area
questions.why: High demand makes the high capacity worth the cost.

questions.q: A city introduces a charge for driving into the centre at peak times. Which result is expected if the charge works as intended?
o: Less peak traffic and more use of other modes
More peak traffic, as drivers pay to enter
No change at all in how people travel
Higher bus fares, applied automatically by the scheme
questions.why: Pricing reduces demand at busy times.

questions.q: A BRT line and a metro both serve a corridor with 8,000 riders per hour at peak. The BRT can carry about 10,000 per hour. What does this suggest?
o: BRT could meet current demand at a lower capital cost, but future growth should be checked
Only a metro can ever work on this corridor
BRT cannot carry passengers at this volume at all
Demand does not matter when choosing between modes
questions.why: Match capacity to present and forecast demand; the cheaper mode may suffice.

questions.q: Critics of congestion pricing often raise which concern?
o: Fairness for lower-income drivers
That it makes the roads wider and busier
That it reduces air quality in the centre
That it changes the map of the city's streets
questions.why: Distributional effects are a main debate; designs may include discounts or reinvestment.

questions.q: A line costs 600 million luns and carries 40,000 passengers a day. Over a 30-year life with 300 operating days a year, what is the capital cost per passenger trip in luns? (Ignore operating costs.)
In a city, 100,000 daily trips are made: 30% by bus. How many bus trips is that?
Match the tool to its purpose.
pairs: Make buses faster and more reliable
questions.why: Each tool targets a different part of the system.

questions.q: A city wants to cut congestion. Explain why adding lanes alone may not work, and name one alternative.
questions.model: New lanes can attract extra traffic so congestion returns; managing demand with pricing, bus priority or better walking and cycling options can move more people with the same space.
questions.why: Induced demand explains why capacity alone may fail.

panel.q: Two proposals cut average commute time by the same amount: one costs 200 million luns and serves 50,000 riders; the other costs 500 million and serves 90,000. Which comparison is most useful?
o: Cost per rider plus access and fairness criteria
Total cost only, with no other information
Ridership only, with no cost shown
The mayor's own preference between the two plans
panel.why: Combine efficiency measures with other stated criteria.

panel.q: How could a city design congestion pricing to address fairness concerns?
panel.model: It could offer discounts or exemptions for low-income residents and people with disabilities and reinvest revenue in buses and safe cycling and walking, so people have real alternatives.
panel.why: Design choices can reduce unfair effects.

panel.q: Which is the best evidence that a new bus lane works?
o: Faster, more reliable journey times and higher ridership
More paint on the road surface along the lane
The number of signs put up beside it
The number of meetings held about the lane
panel.why: Outcome data show the lane's effect.

teach.model: A transport system mixes walking, cycling, buses, trains and cars. Each mode has different cost and capacity, so planners match modes to demand. Adding road lanes can attract more traffic, so cities also manage demand and offer good alternatives.

points.ask: What makes up a transport system?
How do planners pick a mode?
What else can a city do?

stages.title: Environmental regulation
stages.hook: A factory can cut a tonne of pollution for 40 luns, but the fine for polluting is only 25 luns per tonne. What will a rational firm do, and how should the rule be changed?
explain: Environmental regulation sets rules to reduce harm to air, water, land and health. Local governments often handle noise, waste, local air quality, water protection and land-use permits, while national or regional authorities set many standards. The split differs by country.

Regulators use several tools. Command-and-control sets standards or bans. Market-based tools put a price on pollution through taxes or tradable permits under a cap. Information tools require reporting. Subsidies can support clean options. The polluter-pays principle holds that those who cause pollution should bear the cost of dealing with it. The precautionary principle supports acting to prevent serious harm even when evidence is not final.

Good rules are enforceable and proportionate. Penalties must be higher than the cost of compliance or the rule will be ignored. Monitoring, inspections and public data are needed. Regulators weigh costs to business and households against health and environmental benefits, and disagreements about the right balance are normal in democratic societies.

example.q: A firm can cut pollution at 40 luns per tonne. The fine is 25 luns per tonne. For 1,000 tonnes, compare the cost of cutting with the fine. What is the problem?
steps: Paying the fine is cheaper, so the rule gives no incentive to cut.
example.a: Fine is too low; it should exceed 40 luns/tonne.

analogies.home: A parking fine cheaper than a parking space means people ignore the rule.
analogies.farm: Rules on fertiliser run-off protect the stream that all farms downstream depend on.
analogies.sea: Rules on ship discharges protect fish stocks for all fleets.
analogies.nature: A wetland filters water for free; protecting it can cost less than building a plant.

terms: Regulation by setting standards or bans.
A right to emit a set amount, which can be bought and sold under a cap.
Those who cause pollution bear the cost of managing it.
Act to prevent serious harm even when evidence is incomplete.

misc.right: Costs and benefits vary; well-designed rules can protect health and sometimes create jobs, but some firms and workers bear real costs.

stages.limits: Economists and communities disagree about the best tool and stringency; evidence on costs and benefits varies with context.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between a carbon tax and a cap-and-trade system.

questions.q: Which tool puts a price on pollution?
o: A pollution tax
A noise sign
A park bench
A school timetable
questions.why: Taxes and tradable permits create a price.

questions.q: What does the polluter-pays principle say?
o: Those who cause pollution bear the cost of managing it
Residents always pay the whole cost, whoever pollutes
Nobody pays, because pollution is nobody's fault
Governments pay for all of the pollution that happens
questions.why: It assigns responsibility to the source.

questions.q: A fine is lower than the cost of complying. What is likely to happen?
o: Firms may pay the fine and keep polluting
Pollution stops at once, as firms follow the rules
Firms will always comply, whatever the fine
Inspectors become unnecessary, since fines are low
questions.why: Incentives must make compliance cheaper than violation.

questions.q: Why is monitoring needed?
o: Rules are only effective if breaches are detected
It is only decoration added to the reports
Firms enjoy having inspectors visit them often
Pollution is invisible, so it cannot be measured
questions.why: Detection and enforcement make rules credible.

questions.q: A river shows early signs of contamination but studies are incomplete. Which principle supports a cautious interim limit?
o: Precautionary principle
Polluter pays
Open tendering
Zoning
questions.why: It supports acting before certainty when harm could be serious.

questions.q: A firm emits 5,000 tonnes. The permit allows 4,200 tonnes. The fine is 60 luns per excess tonne. What is the total fine in luns?
A cap allows 100,000 tonnes in total and is cut by 4% per year for one year. What is the new cap in tonnes?
Match the tool to the type.
questions.why: Regulators combine tools of different types.

questions.q: A factory says new rules will cost jobs. Describe how a regulator should respond using evidence.
questions.model: The regulator should assess the costs and benefits with data, including health benefits and job effects, consult the firm and workers, consider phasing in the rules or transition support, and publish the reasoning.
questions.why: A balanced evidence-based response weighs both sides.

questions.q: A cap-and-trade system lets firms buy and sell permits under a fixed total. What guarantees the environmental outcome?
o: The total cap on emissions
The number of permits traded
The size of the firms
The price of fuel
questions.why: The cap fixes total emissions; trading finds cheaper cuts.

panel.q: A city must reduce river pollution. Option 1: strict standards on each factory. Option 2: a tradable permit scheme. Which statement is the most reasonable?
o: Both can work; compare cost, certainty of outcome, enforceability and fairness
Only standards can work, since trading is never allowed
Only trading can work, since standards never help
Neither can work, so the city should not try
panel.why: Multiple defensible tools exist; criteria decide.

panel.q: Why can pollution rules affect poorer communities differently, and what can regulators do?
panel.model: Polluting sites are often near lower-income areas, so those residents may face more exposure. Regulators can monitor locally, enforce standards, consult residents and consider fairness when siting facilities.
panel.why: Environmental justice is an equity criterion.

panel.q: Which publication best supports accountability?
o: Public emissions data from monitors
Secret reports
Only annual averages with no detail
Advertising slogans
panel.why: Open data lets the public verify performance.

teach.model: Environmental regulation sets rules to reduce harm to air, water and land. Tools include standards, taxes, tradable permits and reporting. Rules work only if penalties are stronger than the cost of complying and if they are monitored and enforced.

stages.title: Housing policy
stages.hook: Rents in Kestrel Bay rose 18% in two years. Should the city cap rents, build more, or give vouchers? What evidence would settle it?
explain: Housing policy aims to make sure people can find safe, stable homes they can afford. It uses supply-side tools (zoning that allows more homes, faster permits, public or non-profit building) and demand-side tools (rent vouchers, subsidies). Others regulate renting, such as notice periods or rent caps. A common affordability measure is housing cost burden: households spending more than about 30% of income on housing are often described as cost-burdened, though thresholds vary.

Each tool has trade-offs. More supply tends to ease prices over time but takes years. Vouchers help quickly but can raise rents if supply is limited. Rent controls can protect sitting tenants but may reduce new supply or maintenance, depending on design; evidence is mixed and context-specific. Inclusionary zoning requires or encourages a share of new homes to be affordable, which can add affordable units without direct public spending but may affect project viability.

Good housing policy mixes tools, tracks results and protects the most vulnerable. Homelessness, overcrowding and poor-quality housing are separate problems that need targeted responses. Leaders judge policies against stated criteria: effect on affordability, supply, fairness, cost to the budget and speed.

example.q: A household earns 2,000 luns a month and pays 760 luns on housing. Is it cost-burdened by the 30% rule?

analogies.home: If a family has too few chairs, giving each person money for chairs may just raise chair prices unless more chairs are made.
analogies.farm: If grain is scarce, price controls alone leave the shelves empty unless more is grown.
analogies.city: Fast permits are like opening more checkout lanes when queues are long.
analogies.tech: Capacity limits mean demand spikes slow everyone down until capacity grows.

terms: Spending a high share of income on housing.
Rules requiring or encouraging affordable units in new building.
A subsidy a household uses to pay rent.
Rules that limit rent increases or levels.

misc.wrong: There is one policy that solves every housing problem.
misc.right: Problems differ by place and group, and strong results usually come from a mix of tools.

stages.limits: Economists disagree on rent control and other tools, and results depend on design and local markets.

trip.prompt: Find one place that uses inclusionary zoning and what share of units it targets.

questions.q: What does housing cost burden measure?
o: The share of income spent on housing
The size of a home in square metres
The age of the building in years
The distance from home to the workplace
questions.why: It is housing cost divided by income.

questions.q: A voucher programme is introduced in a market with very few vacant homes. What is a risk?
o: Rents may rise, offsetting some of the benefit
Rents always fall, since people have more money
Supply increases at once, as vouchers add homes
Nothing changes for anyone in the market
questions.why: Demand support without supply can push up prices.

questions.q: Which is a supply-side tool?
o: Allowing more homes through zoning
A rent voucher paid to tenants
A rent cap set by the city
A cash grant paid to tenants each month
questions.why: Zoning changes what can be built.

questions.q: What is inclusionary zoning?
o: Rules that encourage or require some affordable units in new projects
A ban on building any new housing in the city
A tax on all the land that is left empty
A bus route plan for new housing areas
questions.why: It uses development to deliver affordable homes.

questions.q: A city wants to help homeless people now and also lower rents over ten years. What is the best structure?
o: Combine targeted support now with policies that increase supply over time
Do only one of these things and stop there
Wait ten years and then decide what to do
Rely on rumours about what has worked elsewhere
questions.why: Different time horizons need different tools.

questions.q: Why is evidence on rent control described as mixed?
o: Results depend on design and local conditions
It is always perfect when it is introduced
It is always harmful whatever the design
No one has ever studied it, so nothing is known
questions.why: Different designs and markets give different outcomes.

questions.q: A development of 800 homes must make 15% affordable. How many affordable homes is that?
Rents rise from 500 luns to 590 luns a month. What is the percentage increase?
Order these households from lowest to highest housing cost burden.
Compare one benefit and one risk of rent caps, using stated criteria such as affordability and supply.
questions.model: A cap can protect current tenants from sudden rises and improve stability, but depending on design it may discourage new building or maintenance, so supply and quality must be monitored.
questions.why: A balanced answer for a contested policy.

panel.q: Which approach best fits an evidence-based, non-partisan housing strategy?
o: Set goals, test a mix of tools in pilots, measure results and adjust
Adopt whichever slogan is the most popular this year
Copy another country exactly, without checking the results
Avoid collecting data, so no one can criticise the plan
panel.why: Pilots and evaluation reduce reliance on ideology.

panel.q: A neighbourhood is being redeveloped and long-term residents fear displacement. Suggest two protections.
panel.model: Give early notice and consultation, provide relocation help or a right to return, and require a share of affordable units so existing residents can stay.
panel.why: Policies can reduce displacement risk.

panel.q: A city lists 5,000 households on a waiting list but builds 200 affordable homes a year. What does this suggest?
o: Current supply of affordable homes is far below need
Housing is solved, as the list is so long
The list is irrelevant to housing planning
Waiting lists are known to lower rents
panel.why: At that rate waiting times will be very long.

teach.model: Housing policy helps people find homes they can afford. Cities can allow more homes to be built, give subsidies or vouchers, or regulate renting. Each tool has trade-offs, so cities use a mix, measure the results and adjust.

stages.title: Disaster preparedness
stages.hook: A '1-in-100-year' flood sounds rare. What is the chance that Kestrel Bay sees at least one in the next 30 years?
explain: Disaster management is often described in four phases: mitigation (reduce the risk, for example by building flood walls), preparedness (plans, drills, supplies, warning systems), response (rescue and relief) and recovery (rebuilding and restoring services). Cities usually do local planning and first response, with national and regional agencies supporting.

Risk is often thought of as hazard (how likely and strong the event is) combined with exposure (who and what is in harm's way) and vulnerability (how easily they are harmed). Reducing any of these lowers risk. A '1-in-100-year' event has a 1% chance in any given year; this does not mean it happens once every century. Over n years the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.99ⁿ.

Preparedness depends on clear communication, tested plans, backup systems and fair attention to people who may find it harder to act, such as people with disabilities, the elderly, people who speak other languages or lack transport. Plans are tested by exercises and updated using lessons from real events. Budget choices compare prevention cost with expected losses and consider equity.

example.q: What is the chance of at least one 1-in-100-year flood in 30 years?
steps: Chance of none in a year = 0.99.

analogies.home: Smoke alarms, an exit plan and a first-aid kit each reduce harm at different stages.
analogies.farm: A farmer builds channels before the rainy season and keeps feed in reserve.
analogies.sea: Harbours use warning flags, lifeboats and drills before a storm arrives.
analogies.sport: Teams practise set plays so they work under pressure.

terms: Actions that reduce the risk of a hazard causing harm.
Planning and readiness before an event.
How easily people or assets are harmed.
Average time between events of a certain size.

misc.wrong: A 100-year flood happens exactly once every hundred years.
misc.right: It has a 1% chance each year; it could happen in consecutive years or not for centuries.

stages.limits: Return periods are estimates based on limited records and changing climates, so they carry uncertainty.

trip.prompt: Find the four phases of emergency management and an example action for each.

questions.q: Which is a mitigation action?
o: Building a flood wall
Handing out blankets after a flood
Searching rubble
Counting damage
questions.why: Mitigation reduces risk before an event.

questions.q: A district has a hospital, many elderly residents and one bridge exit. Which factor is most relevant to vulnerability?
o: Limited evacuation options for people who need help
The name of the district on the map
The colour of the buildings in the district
The number of parks in the district
questions.why: Vulnerability depends on how easily people can protect themselves.

questions.q: What does '1-in-100-year flood' mean?
o: A 1% chance in any given year
It happens exactly every 100 years
It can never happen twice
It happens each century
questions.why: The return period is an average probability, not a schedule.

questions.q: Which action best improves preparedness?
o: Running exercises and fixing problems found
Filing the plan away without anyone reading it
Keeping the plan secret from the staff
Not telling the staff what the plan says
questions.why: Plans must be tested and updated.

questions.q: Why include translated and accessible warnings?
o: People who cannot understand or access a warning cannot act on it
It is only decoration added to the alerts
Warnings are optional, so most people can skip them
Only visitors to the city need those warnings
questions.why: Fair preparedness reaches everyone.

questions.q: A 1-in-50-year flood has a 2% chance each year. What is the probability, as a percentage, of no such flood in the next 2 years? (0.98 × 0.98, rounded to 1 decimal place)
Using the 1-in-100-year flood example, what is the percentage chance of at least one in 30 years (round to the nearest whole number)?
Put the four phases in the usual order.
questions.why: The cycle runs from reducing risk to rebuilding.

questions.q: A flood wall costs 90 million luns and would avoid expected losses of 6 million luns a year. Describe how a city could decide whether to build it.
questions.model: Compare the wall's life-cycle cost with the expected losses it avoids over its life (for example 6 million a year over many decades), check maintenance, risk estimates and alternatives, and consider who is protected and how fairly.
questions.why: Cost-benefit analysis plus equity and uncertainty.

questions.q: Which indicator best shows readiness?
o: Exercise results showing plans work in practice
The number of binders printed for the plan
The number of speeches the mayor has given
The number of posters put up in the city
questions.why: Tested performance is stronger evidence than documents.

panel.q: A city has money for either raising a seawall (benefits a wealthy waterfront) or early-warning sirens and shelters (benefits a poorer low-lying district). Which approach is most defensible?
o: Compare risk reduction, people protected, cost and fairness using evidence
Fund the waterfront because the land there is worth more
Fund only whichever option costs the least
Choose between the options randomly, by drawing lots
panel.why: Use stated criteria, including fair protection.

panel.q: Why are communication plans a core part of preparedness?
panel.model: People can only act if warnings are timely, clear and reach them in languages and channels they use, and if they trust the source.
panel.why: Effective communication enables action.

panel.q: After a disaster the city rebuilds exactly as before. What is a missed opportunity?
o: Building back safer to reduce future risk
Painting the new buildings in the same colours
Hiring workers to do the rebuilding job
Writing a report that nobody ever reads
panel.why: Recovery is a chance to reduce future vulnerability.

teach.model: Disaster management has four phases: mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. Risk depends on how likely the hazard is, who is exposed and how vulnerable they are. Cities test plans, warn everyone clearly and treat vulnerable people fairly.

stages.title: Public policy evaluation
stages.hook: Crime fell in a district after a new programme began. Did the programme cause the fall, or would it have happened anyway?
explain: Policy evaluation asks whether a policy was carried out as planned and whether it achieved its goals. It distinguishes inputs (money and staff), outputs (what was delivered, such as 500 workshops), outcomes (changes for people, such as more employment) and impacts (long-term effects attributable to the policy).

The hard question is causation. A before-and-after comparison can mislead because other things change. Evaluators use a counterfactual: what would have happened without the policy. A comparison group helps. A difference-in-differences estimate subtracts the change in a similar untreated group from the change in the treated group. Randomised pilots are the strongest design where feasible, but not always possible or ethical.

Evaluation also asks about cost-effectiveness (cost per unit of outcome), equity (who benefited), unintended effects and how reliable the data are. Indicators should be defined before the policy starts. Results should be published, whether good or bad, and used to improve or end policies. Politicians and the public often disagree about goals, so evaluation is most useful when criteria are agreed in advance.

example.q: In a treated district, burglaries fell from 120 to 90. In a similar comparison district, burglaries fell from 110 to 98. What is the difference-in-differences estimate?

analogies.home: If you tried a new study routine and your marks rose, you would also check whether the test was easier.
analogies.farm: A farmer tests a new fertiliser on one field and compares it with a similar field without it.
analogies.sport: A coach compares a team that used a new drill with a similar team that did not.
analogies.tech: A/B tests show two groups different versions and compare results.

stages.mnemonic: Goal, Indicator, Baseline, Comparison, Cost: G-I-B-C-C.
terms: What would have happened without the policy.
A change in people's lives or conditions caused by a policy.
Comparing before-and-after change in a treated group with the change in a comparison group.
Cost per unit of outcome achieved.

misc.wrong: If things improve after a policy, the policy worked.
misc.right: Other factors may explain the change; evaluation compares against a counterfactual.

stages.limits: Comparison groups are never perfect, and effects may differ between places, so findings need replication and humility.

trip.prompt: Find what the page says about evaluating whether a policy worked.

questions.q: What is an outcome in policy evaluation?
o: A change in people's conditions caused by the policy
The money spent on running the policy
The number of meetings held about it
A list of the staff who ran it
questions.why: Outcomes measure real-world change.

questions.q: Why is a before-and-after comparison weak evidence on its own?
o: Other factors may have changed at the same time
Time never passes between the two measurements
Data are never collected in either period
It is always correct, so it needs no other evidence
questions.why: Causation needs a counterfactual.

questions.q: Which is an output, not an outcome?
o: 500 training sessions delivered
Higher employment rate among residents of the district
Lower accident rate on the city's streets
Higher average incomes for local households
questions.why: Outputs are what was delivered; outcomes are the changes.

questions.q: Why define indicators before starting a policy?
o: To avoid choosing favourable measures afterward
To delay the start of the policy by some months
To hide the results of the policy later on
To increase the costs of the policy for the city
questions.why: Pre-set indicators reduce bias.

questions.q: A pilot programme is run in randomly chosen schools and not in others. What does this help with?
o: Estimating the policy's effect more credibly
Making the policy cheaper to run for the city
Avoiding the need to collect any data
Increasing the bias in the results on purpose
questions.why: Random assignment makes groups comparable.

questions.q: A treated area's accidents fell from 80 to 62. A comparison area's fell from 75 to 69. What is the difference-in-differences estimate (negative means a bigger fall in the treated area)?
questions.why: Treated −18, comparison −6; −18 − (−6) = −12.

questions.q: A programme costing 2,400,000 luns prevents 160 incidents. What is the cost per incident prevented in luns?
Match the term to its meaning.
questions.why: These distinctions structure evaluations.

questions.q: Crime fell by 10% in a district after a new patrol scheme. Describe two checks before concluding that the scheme caused the fall.
questions.model: Compare with similar districts that did not get the scheme and check earlier trends, other changes such as the economy or reporting practices, and whether the fall persists over a longer period.
questions.why: Causal claims need comparison and checks for alternative explanations.

questions.q: Why should evaluation results be published even if they are unfavourable?
o: Transparency allows learning and accountability
They embarrass staff, so they should be buried
They end all policies once they are published
They are always wrong when they are unfavourable
questions.why: Learning from failures improves future policies.

panel.q: Programme A costs 3,000 luns per outcome and helps a few people with severe needs. Programme B costs 1,000 luns per outcome but helps those who need it least. How should leaders judge?
o: Weigh cost-effectiveness with equity and need using stated criteria
Choose B because it is cheaper per outcome, whoever it helps
Choose A because it is the bigger programme overall
Choose neither programme, and spend nothing at all
panel.why: Cost-effectiveness is one criterion among several.

panel.q: Why can measuring a single indicator cause problems, and what is the remedy?
panel.model: If staff are judged on one number, they may focus on it and ignore other goals or game the figure. Using several indicators, checking quality and auditing data reduces this.
panel.why: Balanced measurement reduces gaming.

panel.q: Which makes an evaluation most credible to people with different political views?
o: Agreed criteria, open data and independent review
Secret methods that only the authors understand
Selecting only the good results to show the public
Using only anecdotes from supporters of the policy
panel.why: Transparent methods build trust across groups.

teach.model: Policy evaluation checks whether a policy was delivered and whether it caused the intended change. Evaluators compare with what would have happened without the policy, for example using a similar comparison group. They also look at cost, fairness and unintended effects.

points.ask: How do we know the policy caused it?
